name: Adam Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Adam, 27. I'm a junior at Brook & Sons, a firm of about fifteen on the industrial estate, and most of our clients are tradespeople: plumbers, roofers, a scaffolding company. I live with my girlfriend Nadia, who's a dental nurse, in a rented flat above a launderette. Money's tight, we've got about three weeks of bills saved if we're lucky.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do bookkeeping and quarterly VAT returns, and in spring I do a lot of the builders' tax returns. The clients drop off van receipts and invoice books, and I key them into the system and reconcile them against the bank. I like the trades clients, they're straight with you, and I like a tidy spreadsheet. What wears me out is the exams; I failed the tax paper in June and I'm resitting in March, and studying after a full day of numbers is hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here is the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because I never trusted it anyway. At work I'd probably say to Steve, the manager, that we can stop talking about new software and get on with the work. I don't post much online, maybe a comment in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it still worries me a bit, because even a small change lands on keying in receipts, which is what I do most. Brook & Sons is careful with money. If a tool saves my manager one junior's hours, I'm the one who failed his exam. On top of that, I'm on low pay, there are only two other firms near here, and Nadia and I can't save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass that tax paper in March, full stop, because it's the thing that makes me safe. I'd do extra Saturdays in the busy season for the overtime. And I'd stop eating out on Fridays and put that £60 a month towards savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. Not because of AI really, but because I've got no room for anything to go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if your hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia's pay covers about half the rent and the food. If I lost a day a week, we'd be short every month by around £250. We'd probably have to ask her parents for help, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never trusted AI. Where did that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A client of ours, a roofer called Gary, used some app to do his own VAT and it got the dates wrong, so he got a fine. I spent two days sorting it out. Since then I'd rather do it by hand and know it's right.

I'd tell Steve we can stop talking **software** and get on with work.
think: Even small automation lands on **keying receipts**, my main job.
I'm the one who **failed his exam**, so I'd be first to lose hours.
do: Pass the **tax paper** in the March resit.
Work extra **Saturdays** in busy season for overtime.
Stop Friday takeaways and save **£60 a month**.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly because there's **no room** for anything to go wrong.
S0.quote: If a tool saves my manager one junior's hours, I'm the one who failed his exam.
fieldNote: Even a mild change hits his **data entry**, and he sees himself as the weakest junior.

steps.text: Resit and pass the professional tax paper in March
Work extra Saturdays at Brook & Sons in the busy season
Stop Friday takeaways and move £60 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here is the card. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to happen whether we like it or not, so firms should be careful how they do it. At work I'd say we still need people to check what the software spits out, because I've seen what happens when nobody does. I'd keep it measured, I'm not one for causing a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in real trouble. Keying, reconciling, drafting VAT returns, that's the checking and planning stuff on the card, and I'm slow and I don't use AI tools. If Steve brings in a system that reads the invoice books, he'd keep the two juniors who can run it, and I'm not one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd force myself to learn the firm's software properly, even though I'd hate it, maybe ask Priyesh, who's good with it, to show me at lunch. I'd pass my exams. And I'd start looking at in-house jobs at bigger trade firms, like the scaffolding company, where they need someone on accounts who knows the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach turns, because I chose accounting as a solid job and I'm already behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really ask Priyesh for help, or is that something you'd put off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put it off, if I'm honest, until Steve made it clear. I don't like looking like I don't know something. But if it was that or my job, I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm doing what I can and that dental nurses aren't going anywhere. Her job's hands-on, and people still want a person in their mouth, not a machine. She'd tell me to stop worrying and study, which is fair.

We still need people to **check the software**.
think: I'm in **real trouble**: slow, junior, and **no AI** use.
Steve would keep the two juniors who can **run the system**.
do: Learn the **firm's software**, asking Priyesh to show me at lunch.
Look for **in-house accounts** jobs at bigger trade firms.
feel: **Alarmed**; I chose a solid job and I'm **already behind**.
S1.quote: I chose accounting as a solid job and I'm already behind.
fieldNote: Public tone is **measured**; private view is that he'd be **first out**.
Would learn tools only **under pressure**, admitting he'd put it off.
Sees his partner's **hands-on job** as the household's safer income.

steps.text: Ask colleague Priyesh to teach the firm's software at lunch
Pass the remaining accountancy exams this year
Apply for in-house accounts jobs at the scaffolding company

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here is the card. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to slow it down, because nobody can adjust in two years. At work I'd probably say we're all in the same boat, even Steve. I'd not say much online, I'd just be reading everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished in accounting by 2029. It's all thinking work, so I don't get the three-year gap the robots give, and I've not even passed my exams. The only real move is to go hands-on, because a plumber or a roofer has until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd ask the trades clients I know, like the scaffolders, if they'd take me on as a labourer or a trainee. I'd cut everything, the car, the phone contract, the gym, and try to get two months saved. Once it arrived, I'd sign on for whatever help there is and probably move in with Nadia's parents to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I've got no plan that adds up and no money to make one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with Nadia's parents. How would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small house, two bedrooms, her younger brother still there. Living on a sofa bed in the front room of my girlfriend's parents' house would be embarrassing, but it saves £750 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'go hands-on'. Do you have any of those skills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I helped my dad tile a bathroom once and it was crooked. I'd be starting at the bottom at 29, and after three years the robots come anyway.

say: The government should **slow it down**; nobody adjusts in two years, I'd say.
I'd say we're **all in one boat**, even the manager.
think: Going hands-on buys until **about 2031**, but I've no trade skills.
do: Ask scaffolding clients for **labourer or trainee** work.
Cut the car, phone and gym to get **two months saved**.
Sign on for help and **move in** with Nadia's parents.
feel: **Panicked**; no plan adds up and there's **no money** to make one.
S2.quote: Living on a sofa bed in the front room of my girlfriend's parents' house would be embarrassing, but it saves £750 a month.
fieldNote: He correctly sees **thinking work** goes first, so a trade buys three years at most.
No **trade skills**, no qualification, and almost no savings leave him overwhelmed.
Fallback is **family**, not the state, though he'd claim help too.

steps.text: Ask the scaffolding client for labourer or trainee work
Sell the car and cancel the phone contract and gym
Claim whatever unemployment help exists once work dries up
Move in with Nadia's parents to save £750 a month rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here is the card. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but enough to do something, if people start now. At work I'd suggest Brook & Sons tells us honestly what it plans. I'd stay fairly quiet about it beyond that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can finish my exams and earn a bit more for a few years. But I'd be qualified in something that mostly goes in 2031, so it's a short win. The extra three years until robots arrive in 2034 would make a trade worth more than in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd pass the tax paper and qualify. By year two I'd start an evening course in electrical work or plumbing at the college, so I've got something hands-on to switch into. I'd put £100 a month away, more after I qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but less frozen. Changing career in five years is like having to change trains, and I don't like changing trains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would you pick, electrical or plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plumbing, probably, because half our clients are plumbers and they're always busy. One of them, Dean, said he'd let me shadow him. He says nobody's building a robot to crawl under a sink yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Nadia's job change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we've got one income that should last past 2034, which makes me braver. I wouldn't do it alone. If she was in an office too, I'd be terrified.

Brook & Sons should be **honest** about its plans.

An extra three years to **2034** makes a **trade** worth learning.

fieldNote: He still expects to **lose his accounting job** by 2031, so mood stays alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Here is the card. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time and people should use it sensibly. At work I'd say the firm should plan who moves where. I'd not make a big thing of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like I could get myself sorted. I'd be 37, qualified, maybe running the trades clients myself, with savings. But I'd still lose the accounting work in 2036, so I'd want a second skill by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, qualify and get the pay rise. Over the next five years I'd save properly, maybe £200 a month, and do a plumbing qualification part-time. By 2033 I'd want to be able to switch, or do both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a slow way. Ten years of warning makes AI a worry for later, not for tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything else, like where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still rent, but maybe we'd try for a mortgage around 2030 if I qualify. Nadia wants a garden. With ten years I'd risk it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if the firm made us, and with ten years I'd have time to get used to them. I'd still check everything by hand at first. Old habits.

The firm should **plan who moves** where.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. I'd be unqualified, untrained in anything else and broke. What would help is a proper funded retraining scheme for people my age, with wages, so I could learn plumbing without losing the flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how many people like me there are. Juniors who aren't the best, who aren't into tech, in towns with two firms. Nobody's planning for the slow, careful ones.

headlineQuote: Nobody's planning for the slow, careful ones.
portrait: Adam is a 27-year-old **junior** doing **bookkeeping** and VAT for tradespeople.
He rents with Nadia, a **dental nurse**, and has about three weeks of savings.
Centre-ground and wary of tech, he **never uses AI** after a client's app-caused fine.
He's anxious even in the plateau, **panicked** at AGI by 2028, and eyes **plumbing** as a fallback.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be unqualified, untrained and **broke**.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded retraining scheme** with wages for people his age.
